transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-11
Time: 15:30 ET / 19:30 UTC
Duration: ~43 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Daniel (Redwood SE), Olivia (CSM), Tom (Solutions), Ravi (Keystone), Elena (Infra), Samir (Product), Aisha (Procurement)

Auto-summary (auto-gen): Quick check on pilot economics; caching shows promising delta; batch sizes need further sweep; procurement requested SOC2 and latency SLOs; action items assigned.

00:00 Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining — quick roll call?
00:06 Ravi: hey, ravi here. elena, samir, aisha on my side.
00:10 Maya: awesome, maya from redwood, daniel se on the call, olivia csm. we have about 40 minutes, main goals: review last week's numbers, caching impact, and decide on the next sweep.
00:22 Daniel: i'll start with the metric summary i sent earlier — apologies if folks haven't opened it yet — tl;dr: baseline single-model route, small-batch default (bs=1), average latency p50 about 230ms, p95 around 740ms, tokens/sec per GPU was ~1,500 at 8 concurrent streams. cost per 1k tokens roughly $0.42 with current quantization profile.
00:45 Elena: can you repeat the tokens/sec/$ number? i missed that.
:47 Daniel: yeah, sorry — about fifteen hundred tokens per second for the cluster we measured, which maps to roughly four thousand tokens per dollar depending on run shape, but the cleaned econ spreadsheet shows 2.9k tokens per dollar when accounting for KV caching and steady-state batching. the short is caching helped.
01:10 Ravi: hold up — 2.9k tokens per dollar sounds like a big jump. where is that from?
01:15 Daniel: that's the observed tokens/dollar when we enabled prefix kv caching on a 50% request overlap workload. cache hit rate hovered 36-42% depending on the prompt set. with hits we avoid full attention recompute for prefixes which saved about 28% in token compute cost.
01:38 Samir: just to be clear, the production prompt mix is a bit different, more short completions, so our real hit rate might be lower.
01:45 Maya: good callout. that's why we asked for the three canonical prompt sets — to run the sweep against realistic mixes.
01:51 Samir: yes, i can upload them after this call.
01:55 Daniel: also important: when we increased batch sizes to 8 and 16 we saw tokens/sec improve, but median latency climbed. sample: bs=1 p50 230ms, bs=8 p50 350ms, bs=16 p50 470ms. p95 for bs=16 spiked near 1.1s in our pilot run under burst.
02:20 Elena: so is the recommendation to keep bs low for user-facing APIs?
02:24 Daniel: depends on SLO. For sub-300ms interactive UX, we recommend bs <= 2 and aggressive early-evict LRU caching. For async tasks or batch jobs, bs 8-16 is more economical.
02:38 Ravi: our SLAs for the customer portal expect 400ms median, 1s p95 — so maybe bs=8 is acceptable but p95 risk worries me.
02:48 Maya: two levers: we can route latency-sensitive traffic to a smaller low-batch pool (dedicated) and route background to a high-batch pool. Redwood can do policy routing — Daniel, can you remind them of the route config?
02:59 Daniel: yeah, routing policy is per-endpoint. you can set priority/latency tags and we route to pools with matching profiles; fallback to lower-cost variants if capacity constrained. We can also pin a model variant with lower quantization for latency-critical calls.
03:20 Ravi: about quantization — are we safe on quality if we pick the int8-fast profile? last run had a few hallucination-ish outputs on the longer prompts.
03:29 Daniel: we did see a small regen rate increase on some long-context eval prompts at int8-fast; when we switched to int8-conservative the token cost rose ~12% but quality improved. We recommended running the regen evals with your three prompt sets.
03:45 Samir: can that be measured automatically in your eval suite?
03:48 Olivia: yes — our eval harness will run regen/ROUGE/semantic-sim on the prompt set and produce a delta table. We'll include that in the sweep report.
03:56 Aisha: procurement question: we need SOC2, data residency note, and a simple network diagram before we can expedite a PO.
04:04 Maya: absolutely — we'll send the SOC2 link and a short VPC diagram. Tom, can you handle the security doc handoff?
04:09 Tom: yes, i'll bundle SOC2, encryption (KMS) notes, and a one-page VPC diagram — will put in Dropbox link.
04:16 Aisha: great. also, price cadence — do you have a committed discount tier if we do a six-month pilot?
04:22 Maya: procurement / pricing is negotiation but we can provide a pilot commitment discount for dedicated pools; i'll send a template.
04:29 Elena: back to metrics — what were the measured cache-hit breakdowns by prompt set? you said 36-42% average. which sets fared best?
04:37 Daniel: the conversational style with longer shared prefixes had the highest hit rate (~42%). Short transactional prompts had lower (~18-22%). The hybrid mixed set we estimated at ~34%. We'll include per-prompt CSV in the report.
04:53 Ravi: okay. does that translate to end-to-end cost saving or is there overhead like cache syncing?
05:00 Daniel: little overhead — the KV cache is in-host and piggybacks on the runtime; small memory overhead per shard but no network sync for our config. For private deployments there are options to share cache across nodes but that's an advanced config we didn't enable for the pilot.
05:18 Samir: curious about warm-up behavior — initial cold starts killed our 95th percentile in the first 10 minutes of the baseline run. did caching help with warm-up?
05:27 Daniel: yes, cache helps fast-path for repeated prefixes — but cold-starts are mostly influenced by instance spin-up and model weights loading. We saw reduced p95 after a steady-state of ~8-12 minutes. For production we recommend pre-warming or standby workers.
05:45 Ravi: thanks. any anomalies in the logs we should watch?
05:48 Daniel: one anomaly — we saw a short GC spike on node 3 during bs=16 run, likely from memory pressure. we've flagged it and will tighten memory limits; that should reduce p95 tail.
06:02 Elena: will that affect tokens/sec numbers?
06:05 Daniel: slightly — reclaiming memory will stabilize throughput; we expect tokens/sec to be consistent but tail latency reduced.
06:12 Maya: next, the econ model: last week we delivered a cost forecast showing three scenarios (baseline, caching enabled, optimized batching). which one are you leaning toward?
06:23 Ravi: i like the optimized batching but worried about UX regressions. can you run a user-facing simulation with bs=4 and targeted cache config?
06:31 Daniel: yes — that's part of the 24-hour sweep we proposed. we'll include bs 1,2,4,8,16 plus with/without prefix caching, and produce per-route SLO curves.
06:44 Samir: please include latency percentiles broken out by prompt type. that's key.
06:48 Daniel: noted.
06:50 Maya: timeline check — we'll run the sweep overnight tomorrow and share raw CSV + summary by midday 2026-04-13. then we propose a debrief on 2026-04-16, does that work?
06:59 Ravi: yes.
07:01 Aisha: procurement: once we get SOC2 + network diagram, we can get internal legal loop started. timeline maybe two weeks.
07:08 Maya: understood. we'll prioritize security docs.
07:11 Olivia: one more ops question — for dedicated capacity, what's the minimum committed?
07:15 Maya: minimum reserved pool is 2 GPUs, but typical pilots start at 4; we can be flexible.
07:21 Elena: for the staging routing test you mentioned, what's the risk of data leakage? we need assurance that logs are segregated.
07:27 Tom: logs are tenant-isolated; we'll provide the logging retention and RBAC policy doc.
07:33 Ravi: okay good.
07:35 Maya: wrapping up, agreed action items: redwood runs sweep, daniel configures cache, elena flips staging route, samir uploads prompt sets, redwood sends security pack. anything else?
07:47 Samir: i'll add a quality gate — if regen delta > 4% we'll stick with conservative quant.
07:52 Daniel: noted and we'll include regen metrics.
07:55 Maya: great. thanks everyone — we'll send the follow-up email with attachments and the sweep schedule. talk soon.
08:03 Ravi: thanks all. bye.
